isochrone:
Network isochrone

A process widget. It draws the area you can reach on foot within a stated time, walking along real streets, from one or more sites.

What it does

From each site it walks outward along the street network until the time runs out, then draws a band around every street it reached. The result is one region per site — not a circle, because streets are not straight and do not go everywhere.

A walk has three parts and this charges for all three: to the nearest junction, along the streets, and off the street at the end to reach a door.

What you connect

ConnectWhat it needs
your sitesthe points to walk from — pumps, clinics, depots
a street networkfrom the Street network widget

Out come polygons, one per site. Draw them on a Map, or count your records into them with Summarize points in polygons.

How to use it

1. Add it from the palette, under Catchments. 2. Connect your sites and a street network. 3. Set the budget. *Minutes* × *metres per minute* is how far someone can walk — 5 minutes at 75 m/min is 375 m of street. 4. Set the final walk off the street — how far from a street someone can get to a door. The band is this wide where there is time left and narrower where there is not. 5. Set the snap limit — how far a site may be from the nearest street before the result says so. 6. Check the zone. Measuring happens in metres, so the UTM zone is part of the answer, and every measuring step in one workflow must agree on it. The run is refused by name if they disagree. 7. Run the workflow, then read the regions on a map and the alert in the Inspector.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat it does there
John Snow · walking catchmentsfive-minute walking regions around the eight Soho pumps, drawn as a plot and as an interactive map, with the 1854 deaths counted into them

What it will not do

  • It is not a service area or a routed travel time. It is an approximation of shape, drawn

to be read. Nobody agreed to it and no router produced it.

  • It assumes the ground beside a street can be walked, at walking speed, in any direction.

Near the edge of the budget that is where the region is most generous.

  • It does not drop a site that is far from the streets. Such a site is routed anyway, with

the straight line to the nearest junction charged against its budget. Its region is marked, the widget glows red, and the Inspector names the leg. That straight line assumes you can cross whatever lies between, so the region reaches further than the ground allows.

  • A site whose walk to the street would spend the whole budget gets no region at all. It

reaches nothing in the stated time, which is the answer. It is named in the alert, and the note on the result says the counts are over the sites that reached something.

The direction it misleads

All of the above push the same way: a poorly connected place looks better served than it is. Streets and footpaths are mapped unevenly, and informal settlements least of all. Read a region over sparsely mapped ground as optimistic, check the alert for sites routed off the network, and check how far each site had to go to reach a street.

Checking it yourself

The lab's snapping notebook measures the displacement on the example data, and the corridor check rebuilds the region from the stated rule with Shapely.
map_output:
Map

An output widget. It draws what your workflow produced. It computes nothing, changes nothing and decides nothing — if a number looks wrong on the map, the step that produced it is where to look.

What it does

A map is a stack of layers, drawn in order from the ground up:

1. a basemap, if you choose one — streets or terrain, under everything else 2. a study area, as the ground your results sit on 3. polygons — catchments, hulls, cells or bands 4. points — your records, sites, or anything with a location 5. a raster or a street network, where you have one

You connect what you want drawn. There is no setting that says what kind of map this is.

What you connect

ConnectTo draw
a study areathe boundary your work is inside
a point layerrecords with locations — up to eight separate layers
catchment polygonsareas reached, covered or grouped
a reasoning resultpoints coloured by the decision a ruleset reached
a coverage checkpoints marked inside, outside or missing a location
a rasterprepared or clipped cells
a street networkthe streets themselves

How to use it

1. Add the Map from the palette, under Outputs. 2. Connect your first layer. Drag from any step that produced something drawable onto the map's + Add a layer port, or pick it from Add a layer in the Inspector. The map works out which port it belongs to. 3. Add more layers the same way. A second point source gets a layer of its own rather than replacing the first. 4. Choose how it is drawn. *Static plot* exports as an SVG with a scale bar and a north arrow. *Interactive map* can be panned and zoomed, and is the only one that can show a basemap. 5. Choose a basemap if the geography matters — streets or terrain under your results. Leaving it at *None* keeps the map working with no connection at all. 6. Title it, and write the source note. Both appear on the map and in its export. 7. Run the workflow. The map appears as a Results tab.

Reading what you get

  • The key names every layer drawn.
  • The scale bar and north arrow appear on a static plot. An interactive map has no

single scale, so it shows neither.

  • The source note carries whatever you wrote, plus the licence of anything the map used.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat the map shows
John Snow · outbreak extentthe judged outline over 250 death locations
John Snow · Voronoi catchmentsone catchment per pump, with deaths overlaid
John Snow · walking catchmentstravel-time bands, as a plot and as an interactive map
Old Naledi · diagnostic accessfacilities coloured by the decision a ruleset reached
Old Naledi · raster clippinga clipped raster inside its boundary
Manila · coastal exposurefacilities with their assigned projection site
Geoprivacythe same records before and after being moved

What it will not do

  • It cannot draw everything at once. A map with both a raster and polygons connected draws

the raster. The layers stay connected; only one is drawn.

  • It cannot reorder or restyle layers. Draw order is fixed, and so are the colours.
  • A basemap is not included in the SVG export. The tiles come from an outside service as

you look at the map, so a figure you export shows your layers on a blank ground.

  • Choosing a basemap sends the area you are viewing to that service. Everything else about

this map works offline. For maps of sensitive locations that is worth knowing before you switch it on.

  • It cannot tell you whether a map is honest. Emphasis, framing and colour all change how a

map reads, and none of them changes a number. See the layers you connected, and say in the source note what the map is about.
snap_to_network:
Snap to network

A process widget. It moves each of your sites onto the nearest junction of a street network, so that steps which travel along streets have somewhere to start.

What it does

A route has to begin on the street network. Your sites almost never sit exactly on a junction — a pump is in a yard, a clinic is set back from the road — so this widget finds the nearest junction to each one and puts it there.

It also records how far each site moved, which is the number to watch.

What you connect

ConnectWhat it needs
your sitesthe points to move
a street networkfrom the Street network widget

Out come the same sites, at junctions, each carrying the distance it travelled. Feed them to Reachable junctions or a walking-catchment step.

How to use it

1. Add it from the palette, under Catchments. 2. Connect your sites and a street network. 3. Set the snap limit — how far a site may be from the network before the result says so. 4. Run the workflow, then read the snap distances in the output or the Inspector.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat it does there
John Snow · walking catchmentsputs the eight pumps onto the Soho street network before travel times are computed

What it will not do

  • It will not leave your data where it was. Every site comes out at a junction. The output

is derived data, not observations any more, and the furthest any site moved is recorded in the run evidence.

  • It will not drop a site that is far from the network. A site past the snap limit is still

moved to its nearest junction and is marked: its first leg crosses ground no street covers. The widget glows red on the canvas and the Inspector lists each one with its distance. The limit decides whether the result says so, not whether the site is in it.

  • It will not tell you the move was acceptable. If a site travelled 200 m to reach a

junction, everything measured afterwards starts 200 m from where it should, and that error appears nowhere in the final numbers. Check the snap distance every time.

When sites are marked, you have three honest options: raise the limit, extend the street network where it stops short, or accept the list and say so in what you publish.

Checking it yourself

The lab's snapping notebook checks the junction choice against pyproj and measures each displacement against a five-minute walking budget — one of the eight example pumps was decided by 0.43 m.
summarize_hull:
Observed extent (convex hull)

A process widget. It takes points and gives back one polygon: the smallest convex outline that contains them, with the area it encloses.

What it does

Stretch an elastic band around all your points and let it go. The shape it settles into is the convex hull — the outline of where your observations are, with no dents.

Along with the shape you get two measurements the rest of your workflow can read: the area it encloses, in square metres, and its span, the distance across its longest axis.

What you connect

ConnectWhat it needs
a point layerat least three points that have locations

Out comes one polygon. Connect it to a Map to see it, a Table to read its numbers, or a Ruleset to make a judgement about its size.

How to use it

1. Add it from the palette, under Summaries. 2. Connect a point layer. Points without a location sit the step out, and the notes say how many took part. 3. Check the zone. The widget measures in metres, so it projects your points first, and the UTM zone it uses is part of the answer. The Inspector suggests the zone that fits your data and tells you what a different one would cost. 4. Run the workflow, then read the area on the output or draw the outline on a map.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat it does there
John Snow · outbreak extentoutlines the 250 death locations, and a ruleset judges whether the outbreak extent is large enough to look at

What it will not do

  • It will not follow the shape of your data. A hull is convex, and cases along a river or

facilities along a coast are not. The outline fills in the space between them, so it claims ground where nothing was observed. If that matters, do not use a hull.

  • It is not a boundary. It is an outline of what was *seen* — not a service area, not a

catchment, not anything anyone agreed to. Where your observation stopped is not where the thing you were observing stopped.

  • Three points in a line enclose nothing, and the widget refuses rather than returning an

area of zero.

  • Watch the span against the area. A hull much longer than it is wide is close to a line

and should be read as one. The widget says so in its notes when it happens.

Checking it yourself

The lab's hull notebook recomputes the outline and the area with Shapely and compares them to this widget's.
